blocks.text: That the Syriac word means cat, and not weasel, was recently argued by Geo. Guil. Kirsch in the Preface to the Chronicle of Gregory Barhebraeus translated into Latin, p. VIII. He was moved by two passages of Barhebraeus in which he judges that no meaning other than cat fits the word ܟܟܘܣܬܐ. One of these passages is on p. 216, line 16 of the Syriac text, where Barhebraeus speaks of a great famine that arose in the region of Khorasan: So great was the famine that a litra of bread was sold for one gold denarius, and people ate dogs and ܟܟܘܫܬܐ. On these words Kirsch remarks: "Since the meaning weasel hardly fits, it is not difficult to guess what ܟܟܘܫܬܐ was. Yet this passage, which would not settle the matter, [II, 436] should be compared with another, much clearer one, which leaves no room for doubt. On p. 268, line 4, he describes a famine that afflicted above all the city of Damascus, of whose inhabitants, who numbered 300,000 before the famine, he reports that only 3,000 survived it. He then continues: Because of this failure of the grain supply the mice, troublesome to people, increased beyond measure, because the ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ were lacking, having long since been eaten by the people. Since ܥܘܟܒܪ̈ܐ are by general agreement mice, it is evident without my pointing it out that ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ means cat, the animal more hostile to mice than any other. Although I do not deny that weasels also hunt mice, everyone will think of the cat as soon as the question arises which kind of animal, when lacking, lets mice multiply." So Kirsch. Against this, however, Lorsbach rightly objected, in the book entitled Archiv für die morgenländische Litteratur, vol. 1, p. 204, first, the corresponding Chaldee word כרכושתא, which Bochart has amply proved on this very page to mean weasel, not cat. The name was aptly given to the weasel from its agile and swift movement, for כרכש, كركس [karkas], means he moved, drove to and fro. As to the point on which Kirsch's view chiefly rests, that mice multiplied when the animals called ܟܪܟܘܫܬܐ were lacking, Lorsbach answers well that weasels hunt mice no less than cats do, indeed better, because the slenderness of their bodies lets them get into mouse-holes more easily.

But J. D. Michaelis, on the Syriac Lexicon of Castell which he edited, p. 297, argues that the Syriac ܚܘܠܕܐ means a kind of lizard. His only argument is that at Levit. XI, 30 the Syriac translator put this word for the Hebrew כח, which means lizard. Others, however, will hardly accept this. For the Arabic dialect stands in favour of the mole: that خُلْدٌ [khuld] is the mole is perfectly clear from what Bochart will next adduce from the Arabs.

In the passage of Proverbs, however, Michaelis thinks this word was put, by an error either of a scribe or of an editor, for ܚܘܪܓܐ, "as the Chaldee too, which in Proverbs is almost identical with the Syriac and derived from it, has חורלי."

The same features are observed in the kind of mole peculiar to Asia, which Guldenstaedt described in the Act. Academ. Petropol. vol. 14, p. 409, under the name Spalax Microphtalmus. Cf. Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 2, ch. 4, p. 51. 52.

What Bochart cites from Abdollatif is taken from his great work on Egyptian matters, divided into 13 books. Its Compendium, made by Abdollatif himself, was recently edited in Arabic from a Bodleian manuscript by Jos. White, Professor of Arabic at Oxford.
The reasoning of the ancient versions was carefully examined by J. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 876, and vol. 6, p. 2042. Cf. our note on Ies. II, 20.

Koppe held (in his notes on Lowth's Commentary on Isaiah) that the word חפרפר means two-legged jumping mice, without adequate reason; for this he was also criticized by Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. 3, p. 876, who himself attempted other explanations, though no more certain ones. Oedmann, in the Vermischte Sammlungen, fascicle 3, p. 82. 83, interpreting the Hebrew word as spy of the cows, argues that it means a certain night-roving bird which, according to the fable, sucks the udders of cows: in Linnaeus it is called Caprimulgus (Europaeus), [II, 451] in German Nachtrabe. This seems more learned than probable or suited to the passage of Isaiah. More satisfying is what Paulus offered in the Clavis Philolog. in Iesaiam. He thinks it should be written as two words, לחפר פרות, which he renders into the holes of field mice (חפר, something dug out, a hole, Arab. حُفْرٌ [ḥufr], and פר, a field mouse or mountain mouse, after the Arabic فَأْر [faʾr]). In favour of this interpretation is the fact that לחפר פרות is found written together as one word in only a few manuscripts.
